Dicots. These are flowering plants with two cotyledons, or seed leaves, and they comprise roughly seventy percent of all angiosperm diversity. Dicots include most of the broadleaf trees and shrubs you know, as well as most herbaceous flowering plants, from oaks and roses to beans and daisies. They dominate temperate and tropical forests across the planet.

That pair of cotyledons affects how the seedling develops and how the roots and shoots are structured. When you look at a dicot leaf, it typically has reticulate venation, which is a branching vein network that forms a web-like pattern, quite different from the parallel venation of monocots. Inside the stem, vascular bundles are arranged in a ring around the center, with a clear cortex and pith, and this arrangement supports strong secondary growth, which is how wood forms.

In terms of roots, many dicots develop a deep taproot system with one central root and branches extending from it, which lets established plants access water deep in the soil. Some dicots do develop fibrous roots, but the taproot is characteristic. Their flower parts typically come in multiples of four or five, so you might see five petals, five sepals, and many stamens.

Dicots include most broadleaf forest trees like oaks, maples, and beeches, and most wildflowers you encounter. They include legumes like beans, peas, and clovers, and the composite flowers like daisies and sunflowers. They develop secondary xylem, or wood, through a structure called the vascular cambium. Together, dicots and monocots comprise nearly all flowering plants, making these two groups the foundation of angiosperm diversity.
